Seasonal description: Marron feature among the freshwater foods associated with Birak. Their presence connects the warm, drying season with the rivers and pools that support aquatic life. This is a traditional seasonal resource association, rather than a suggestion that marron occur only during these months.

Sea mullet form part of the fishing resources associated with Birak along the coast, rivers and estuaries. They provide a connection between the season and life around waterways. Mederong is recorded for sea mullet, allowing this entry to describe a particular species rather than mullet generally.

Bream are among the fish associated with Birak fishing, and Paarndi is used for black bream in the Albany and Denmark area. These fish are closely associated with estuaries, where fresh and salty water meet. Their seasonal significance relates to fishing and resource use, rather than a short period of presence.

During Boonaroo, zamia seeds ripen and their fleshy coverings change from green towards bright red. The plant is a cycad that produces cones rather than flowers or ordinary fruit. Its seasonal relationship with emus offers a visible link between plant reproduction and animal feeding. Untreated seeds are not safe to eat.

Marri's pale flower clusters can be prominent during Bunuru, although flowering can extend from December or January through May. This longer season brings flowers into both summer and autumn. The blossom also provides an important food resource for native insects, making a flowering marri a rewarding place to watch insect activity.

As zamia seeds ripen in Bunuru, emus feed on their fleshy outer coverings. This connects the seasonal change in seed colour with a change in food available to animals. The relationship is a feeding event, rather than an emu breeding indicator, and does not mean the seeds are safe for people to eat untreated.

Australian herring are recorded as plentiful during Bunuru, when fishing near the coast and waterways forms an important seasonal association. These fish link the hottest part of the year with coastal food resources. Ngarilang is a Yuat name, which should retain that regional identity in a broad south-west account.

The coastal salmon run can overlap late Bunuru and Djeran, but its timing differs between regional accounts. A Yuat account describes a March-to-May run, while a Nyoongar account places it in April and May. Large moving schools make this a striking seasonal event, with local timing more informative than a single date.

Around Bunbury and Koombana Bay, bottlenose dolphin calves tend to be born between February and May, spanning Bunuru and Djeran. Young calves may be seen travelling beside their mothers. This describes a local calving pattern, rather than a birthing season shared by every dolphin population across the south-west.

Red-flowering gum can continue to display red-orange blossom during Djeran, linking the cooler season with a vivid flowering display. Its flowering period also includes the earlier summer months, so it is not an autumn-only sign. Naturally occurring populations are concentrated towards the south coast, while planted trees occur more widely.

Reddish reproductive structures and woody cones on sheoaks are described among the signs of Djeran. Their colour adds to the season's noticeable changes in plants. The reddish appearance should not be confused with a fungal rust disease, and flowering can extend well beyond Djeran into the following seasons.

Djeran is strongly associated with the salmon run, when large coastal schools take part in a spawning migration. Fish gather around the south-west, with spawning occurring mainly between Cape Leeuwin and Busselton in late autumn and early winter. Ocean currents then help carry eggs and larvae east towards nursery areas.

White flowers may begin appearing on peppermint trees near the end of Makuru. Flowering can continue from July through December, making this an early stage of a much longer display. Wonil is a Wadjuk name for peppermint, and local trees may flower at different times within that broad window.

During Makuru, black swans gather around waterways and prepare to nest. Breeding in southern Australia can continue through Djilba, so nesting and young birds may be seen across both seasons. Water availability also matters: swans may remain at permanent wetlands or move elsewhere when seasonal wetlands become dry.

Southern right whales visit southern coastal waters during the colder months, linking Makuru with a seasonal return to the coast. Sheltered bays provide places for breeding, birth and nursing. This association continues through Djilba and may extend further into spring, especially where mothers and calves remain in nursery areas.

Kangaroos feature among the land-based food resources associated with Makuru, when seasonal accounts describe a greater emphasis on inland resources. The western grey kangaroo is one species represented in this broader relationship. Its inclusion reflects seasonal resource use, rather than a claim that kangaroos are present or breed only in winter.

Jarrah produces pale flowers during the spring and early-summer period, with records for the typical subspecies extending from August to December. Flowering is better shown across Djilba, Kambarang and Birak than as a reliable Bunuru peak. Local timing varies, so observing nearby trees gives a more useful picture than a fixed date.

Bull banksia may begin flowering in late Djilba, with its large pale flower spikes continuing through spring and into early summer. The display can span several Noongar seasons. Large, deeply toothed leaves help identify the tree before the flowers appear and make it easy to follow the same plant through the year.

Orange wattle produces bright yellow flower heads during late winter and spring, contributing to the yellow displays associated with Djilba. Its flowering period can overlap Kambarang as warmer conditions develop. Despite the common name, the flowers are yellow, making colour and season useful starting points for recognising the plant.

Rigid wattle adds yellow flowers to the Djilba landscape, with flowering recorded during August and September. Its display overlaps the transition between cold, wet days and warmer spells. Following the same patch through the season reveals how individual plants begin and finish flowering at slightly different times.

As Djilba progresses, developing grass-tree flower stalks can mark the approach of Kambarang. Watching a stalk emerge offers a way to notice a seasonal transition before the full flowering display. Grass trees include several species across the south-west, so the timing and appearance should be interpreted in a local setting.

Djilba is associated with willie wagtails raising young in the cited Nyoongar seasonal account. Adults can be busy tending nests and protecting their territory, sometimes challenging much larger birds. Their spring activity offers an accessible way to notice the season in gardens, parks and bushland without approaching or disturbing a nest.

White-cheeked honeyeaters are associated with breeding during Djilba in a Nyoongar account. They feed on flower nectar, connecting bird activity with the surrounding plants. Tjoodik can include the New Holland honeyeater within the cultural grouping, so the language name and a photographed bird's scientific identification need not describe exactly the same grouping.

During Djilba, magpies may be building nests, feeding young and defending their family territory. Some adults swoop when they perceive a threat, but many do not. The activity can continue into Kambarang, making parental care a more useful seasonal description than suggesting all magpies become aggressive or remain confined to nests.

Black bream are recorded as a fishing resource during Djilba. Their estuarine habitat connects this seasonal association with waterways that contain changing mixtures of fresh and salty water. Paarndi is documented in the Albany and Denmark area, giving the entry a regional language connection as well as a seasonal one.

The southern right whale association continues through Djilba, when mothers and calves may occupy sheltered south-coast bays. These coastal nursery areas offer a different setting from the whales' wider ocean journeys. Some remain into October, so the observation can overlap Kambarang rather than ending at a calendar boundary.

Possums are documented among the traditional food resources associated with Djilba. This links the season with land-based animals as well as spring flowers and birds. Ngwir is used for possums, but the name alone does not establish which biological species is intended, so this entry remains at the broader possum level.

Kangaroo paws contribute to the colour of Kambarang's wildflower season, alongside other flowering plants across the south-west. Different species have their own flowering periods, so local identification matters. Kurulbrang is documented for the red-and-green kangaroo paw, which can be used as a specific example within this wider group.

Balga flower spikes are associated with Kambarang, particularly following fire. Flowering in Xanthorrhoea preissii can also occur outside these months, with local records extending from June to December. The seasonal display is therefore best understood as a notable period of flowering rather than a guarantee that every plant will bloom at the same time.

Moodjar's bright orange-yellow flowers can appear during Kambarang and continue into Birak, signalling the approach of hotter weather in seasonal accounts. Flowering commonly spans October to January. Beneath the display, this root-parasitic tree connects with other plants underground, adding another ecological relationship to its striking seasonal presence.

Marron are among the freshwater food resources associated with Kambarang. Smooth marron can occur in several colours, including a striking cobalt-blue form, but blue marron are not a separate species. This entry shares its scientific identity with the Birak marron entry while describing a different seasonal resource association.

Dugites become more active as spring conditions warm, fitting the broader increase in reptile activity during Kambarang. They occur in a range of bushland habitats, including drier areas. Their activity is an ecological sign of warming conditions rather than proof of a precise seasonal boundary, and encounters can also occur at other times.

Warmer conditions favour reptile activity and foraging, making Gould's sand monitor a suitable animal to watch for during Kambarang. This is a broad ecological connection rather than a narrowly defined seasonal event. Kaarda can refer to different goannas in different language contexts, so the species identification should follow the animal being described.

Tiger snakes can become more active during spring and are often associated with wetlands and other moist habitats. They may also bask during suitable weather at other times of year. Their Kambarang connection reflects seasonal activity, while Noorn can mean snake generally rather than uniquely identifying the tiger snake.

Warmer conditions favour bobtails basking and foraging after reduced winter activity. Their thick, short tails store reserves that help them through colder periods. Bobtails also give birth to live young, adding interest to a familiar local reptile. The Kambarang link describes seasonal activity rather than an exclusive period of presence or birth.
